title: Object storage: blobs out of the database
summary: Buckets and keys, why files do not belong in the database or through the API, presigned direct uploads, multipart limits, a CDN in front of the bucket, lifecycle tiers, and the commands to drive it.

steps.title: What object storage is
body: Object storage (Amazon S3 and the many S3-compatible stores, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage) keeps
**objects**: a key, the bytes, and a little metadata, in a **bucket**.
```text
bucket: photos-example
users/42/2026/11/9f3c.jpg      2.1 MB   image/jpeg
users/42/2026/11/9f3c_w320.jpg  38 KB   image/jpeg
- **Flat namespace.** `users/42/` is a key prefix, not a folder. Listing by prefix works; renaming a "folder"
means copying every object.
- **Whole objects.** You put and get whole objects (or byte ranges); you do not update the middle of one.
- **Consistency.** S3 has given strong read-after-write consistency for puts, overwrites and lists since
December 2020. Check your store's documentation: not every S3-compatible product promises the same.
- **Cheap and huge, not fast to first byte.** Storage costs cents per GB-month and throughput scales out, but a
GET usually takes tens of milliseconds before the first byte. S3 documents at least 3,500 writes and 5,500
reads per second **per prefix**, so spread hot data over prefixes.
**Why not in the database?** A 2 MB photo in a row bloats backups and replicas, fills the buffer cache with
bytes nobody queries, and makes every replica copy it. Put the bytes in a bucket and the **key plus
metadata** (owner, size, content type, checksum) in the database.

steps.prompt: A social app stores 4 MB profile photos for 30 million users. Where do the bytes and the metadata go?
options: Bytes in object storage behind a CDN; key, owner, size and checksum in the database
Bytes in a `bytea`/`varbinary` column next to the user row, so one transaction covers both
Bytes on the app servers' local disks, with sticky sessions
Bytes in the cache cluster, so reads are fast
steps.explain: That is about 120 TB of photos. In the database it would dominate backups, replicas and memory. Local disks vanish with the server and break when traffic moves. A cache is memory priced for hot data, not a store of record.

steps.title: Presigned URLs: upload around your servers
body: If every upload streams **through** your API, your servers spend their network cards on bytes. 300 uploads
per second of 2 MB is 600 MB/s, about 4.8 Gbps. Let the client upload **directly** to the bucket instead:
```text
1. client ──POST /uploads {size, type}──> API        (auth, quota, picks the key)
2. API    ──signs a URL: PUT users/42/9f3c.jpg, expires in 15 min──> client
3. client ──PUT bytes──────────────────────────────> bucket   (your servers never see them)
4. bucket ──"object created" event──> queue ──> thumbnail worker, then marks the photo ready
A **presigned URL** carries the method, the key, an expiry and a signature made with a secret only your
service holds. The store checks the signature and the clock; anyone holding the URL can do exactly that one
thing until it expires. Keep expiries short, sign the content type and length where the store supports it,
and never trust the upload until the event arrives and a worker has checked the object.

steps.prompt: Put the direct-upload flow in order.
lines: The client asks the API for an upload slot with the file's size and type
The API checks the user and quota, picks a key and returns a short-lived presigned PUT URL
The client PUTs the bytes straight to the bucket
The bucket emits an object-created event onto a queue
A worker validates the file, makes thumbnails and marks the photo ready in the database
steps.explain: The API only ever handles small JSON. The heavy bytes go client to bucket, and the slow work (thumbnails) happens behind a queue.

steps.title: Big files, CDN and lifecycle
body: **Multipart upload** splits a large object into parts that upload in parallel and can be retried one by one.
The S3 limits, which most compatible stores copy:
| Limit | Value |
| part size | 5 MiB to 5 GiB (the **last** part may be smaller) |
| parts per upload | at most 10,000 |
| object size | up to 5 TiB |
| single PUT | up to 5 GiB |
So a big file needs a part size of at least `size / 10,000`. Unfinished multipart uploads keep their parts
(and you pay for them) until aborted: add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete uploads after a few days.
**Serve reads through a CDN.** Point the CDN at the bucket as its origin, use long cache lifetimes with
content-hashed or versioned keys (`9f3c_w320.jpg` never changes), and keep the bucket private to the CDN.
**Lifecycle tiers.** Most photos are hot for days and then rarely read: move old objects to an
infrequent-access or archive class. Archive classes are cheap to keep and slow or costly to read back, so
never archive what users still open.

steps.prompt: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: A time-limited, signed permission for one method on one key
Parallel, retryable parts that the store joins into one object
The part of a key used like a folder, and the unit request limits apply to
Moves, expires or aborts objects by age automatically
Where the CDN fetches on a miss: here, the bucket

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: queues, streams, buckets and search
steps.body: The commands you reach for when a pipeline is behind, an upload misbehaves or search looks wrong.

toolkit.what: Prints a presigned GET URL for an object, to test a download link or hand a file to someone briefly.
flags: seconds until the URL stops working (default 3600)
point the CLI at an S3-compatible store
toolkit.when: checking that a stored object is really there and readable

toolkit.what: Starts a multipart upload and returns its `UploadId`; `upload-part` and `complete-multipart-upload` finish it.
flags: stored with the object and sent back on GET
toolkit.example: aws s3api create-multipart-upload --bucket backups-example --key db/2026-11-27.dump --content-type application/octet-stream
toolkit.when: reproducing a client's failed large upload step by step

toolkit.what: Lists uploads that were started and never completed or aborted: parts you are still paying for.
toolkit.when: the storage bill is higher than the objects you can see

toolkit.what: Shows each partition's committed offset, log-end offset, lag and which member owns it.
toolkit.when: a pipeline is behind: is it every partition (throughput) or one (hot key, stuck consumer)?

toolkit.what: Lists queues with the columns you ask for: depth, unacked and consumer count.
toolkit.example: rabbitmqctl list_queues -p /shop name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers
toolkit.when: a work queue is growing: no consumers, slow consumers, or a poison message

toolkit.what: Queries an Elasticsearch or OpenSearch index directly, bypassing your app, to see what the index really holds.
flags: the query is a JSON body
the same endpoint family, returning only the number of hits
toolkit.when: a product exists in the database but users cannot find it

steps.prompt: Make a download link for the backup that stops working after 10 minutes.
steps.explain: `aws s3 presign` signs a GET for the object; `--expires-in` is in seconds. The link works for anyone who has it, so keep it short-lived.

prompt: **Symptom first.** Since the app added video clips, the API pods run at 30% CPU but p99 has tripled, and
the database grows by 40 GB a day. The dashboard:
code: api pods      cpu 31%   net rx 9.1 Gbps of 10 Gbps   p99 2.4 s
orders-db     cpu 48%   storage +40 GB/day           replica lag 35 s
uploads/s     220 at peak, average clip 5 MB
options: Uploads stream through the API into the database: move to presigned direct uploads to a bucket and keep only keys in the DB
The API needs more CPU: double the pod size
The database needs a bigger disk
Add a cache in front of the API
steps.explain: 220 × 5 MB is 1.1 GB/s, about 8.8 Gbps: the network cards are full while CPU idles. The same bytes land in the database, so storage and replication lag grow. Direct uploads take the bytes off both.

steps.title: Plan a multipart upload
prompt: Write `long[] PlanParts(long size, long preferredPart)` that returns the size of every part, in order:
- `size` must be from 1 byte to 5 TiB, else throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`;
- start from `preferredPart`, clamped to 5 MiB .. 5 GiB;
- if that would need more than 10,000 parts, use the smallest **whole number of MiB** that fits in
- every part has that size except the last, which holds the rest.
`PlanParts(100 MiB, 8 MiB)` is twelve parts of 8 MiB and one of 4 MiB. (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes.)
solution: for (var i = 0; i < count; i++) parts[i] = Math.Min(part, size - i * part);
hints: `Math.Clamp(preferredPart, 5 * MiB, 5 * 1024 * MiB)`, and the part count is a rounded-up division: `(size + part - 1) / part`.
Too many parts? The smallest size that fits is `size / 10,000` rounded up, then rounded up again to a whole MiB.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoMiB = 1024L * 1024;
var dojoP = PlanParts(100 * dojoMiB, 8 * dojoMiB);
Dojo.Eq("100 MiB in 8 MiB parts: 13 parts", 13, dojoP.Length);
Dojo.Eq("the first part is 8 MiB", 8 * dojoMiB, dojoP[0]);
Dojo.Eq("the last part holds the rest: 4 MiB", 4 * dojoMiB, dojoP[^1]);
Dojo.Eq("a 1 MiB preference is raised to the 5 MiB minimum", 20, PlanParts(100 * dojoMiB, dojoMiB).Length);
Dojo.Eq("a 10 GiB preference is capped at 5 GiB", 5 * 1024 * dojoMiB, PlanParts(20L * 1024 * dojoMiB, 10L * 1024 * dojoMiB)[0]);
var dojoBig = PlanParts(1024L * 1024 * dojoMiB, 8 * dojoMiB);
Dojo.Eq("1 TiB: parts grow to 105 MiB", 105 * dojoMiB, dojoBig[0]);
Dojo.Check("1 TiB: no more than 10,000 parts", dojoBig.Length <= 10_000, $"got {dojoBig.Length}");
Dojo.Eq("1 TiB: the parts add up to the file", 1024L * 1024 * dojoMiB, dojoBig.Sum());
Dojo.Eq("exact fit: no tiny last part", 2, PlanParts(10 * dojoMiB, 5 * dojoMiB).Length);
Dojo.Eq("a small file is one part", 1, PlanParts(1000, 8 * dojoMiB).Length);
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("over 5 TiB is refused", () => PlanParts(5L * 1024 * 1024 * dojoMiB + 1, 8 * dojoMiB));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("an empty file is not a multipart upload", () => PlanParts(0, 8 * dojoMiB));

steps.title: Sign and verify an upload URL
prompt: Build a small presigned-URL scheme (generic, not any provider's exact format). The string to sign is
`method + "\n" + path + "\n" + expires`, signed with HMAC-SHA256 and the secret (both as UTF-8), as
- `string Sign(string secret, string method, string path, long expires)`.
- `string Presign(string secret, string method, string path, long expires)` returns
- `bool Verify(string secret, string method, string url, long now)`: true only when `expires` and `sig` are
both present, `now <= expires`, and the signature matches the method, the URL's path and `expires`.
Compare signatures with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals` so timing does not leak how much matched.
Times are Unix seconds passed in, so the tests do not depend on the clock.
starter: string Sign(string secret, string method, string path, long expires)
string Presign(string secret, string method, string path, long expires)
bool Verify(string secret, string method, string url, long now)
solution: string Sign(string secret, string method, string path, long expires)
string Presign(string secret, string method, string path, long expires)
bool Verify(string secret, string method, string url, long now)
if (!query.TryGetValue("expires", out var exp) || !long.TryParse(exp, out var expires)) return false;
if (!query.TryGetValue("sig", out var sig)) return false;
var expected = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(Sign(secret, method, uri.AbsolutePath, expires));
hints: `HMACSHA256.HashData(key, data)` returns the MAC bytes; `Convert.ToHexString(...).ToLowerInvariant()` makes the hex.
In `Verify`, `new Uri(url)` gives `AbsolutePath` and `Query`; split the query on `&` and `=`, then re-sign and compare.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoKey = "test-signing-key";

var dojoExpected = Convert.ToHexString(System.Security.Cryptography.HMACSHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(dojoKey), Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("PUT\n/users/42/9f3c.jpg\n1800000900"))).ToLowerInvariant();
Dojo.Eq("Sign uses method, path and expiry in that order", dojoExpected, Sign(dojoKey, "PUT", "/users/42/9f3c.jpg", 1800000900));
var dojoUrl = Presign(dojoKey, "PUT", "/users/42/9f3c.jpg", 1800000900);
Dojo.Eq("Presign builds the URL", "https://files.example.com/users/42/9f3c.jpg?expires=1800000900&sig=" + dojoExpected, dojoUrl);
Dojo.Check("a fresh URL verifies", Verify(dojoKey, "PUT", dojoUrl, 1800000000));
Dojo.Check("it still works at the expiry second", Verify(dojoKey, "PUT", dojoUrl, 1800000900));
Dojo.Check("an expired URL is refused", !Verify(dojoKey, "PUT", dojoUrl, 1800000901));
Dojo.Check("a PUT URL cannot be used for DELETE", !Verify(dojoKey, "DELETE", dojoUrl, 1800000000));
Dojo.Check("another key (path) is refused", !Verify(dojoKey, "PUT", dojoUrl.Replace("9f3c", "0000"), 1800000000));
Dojo.Check("a stretched expiry is refused", !Verify(dojoKey, "PUT", dojoUrl.Replace("1800000900", "1900000900"), 1800000000));
Dojo.Check("a different secret is refused", !Verify("other-key", "PUT", dojoUrl, 1800000000));
Dojo.Check("no signature is refused", !Verify(dojoKey, "PUT", "https://files.example.com/users/42/9f3c.jpg?expires=1800000900", 1800000000));
